fm01_gaikuang.note: Wenshi ziliao xuanji, the serial publication of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference's historical-materials committee, begun in 1960. It solicited first-person accounts from former Nationalist officials, officers and businessmen — many of them, like Shen Zui, recently pardoned prisoners. Almost the whole of this book first appeared there. The series is indispensable and partisan at once: it preserves testimony that exists nowhere else, and it was commissioned, edited and published by the state the witnesses had fought against, in a period when the value of a memoir was measured partly by how thoroughly its author condemned his former self.

Wen Qiang (1907–2001), Shen Zui's colleague in the Juntong and later a Nationalist lieutenant general; captured at the Huai-Hai campaign in 1949, held as a war criminal and pardoned in 1975, the last group released. He was a distant cousin of Mao Zedong on his mother's side. The word "Comrade" here is doing real work: by the time Shen Zui wrote, Wen Qiang had been rehabilitated into the same CPPCC apparatus that published them both.

fm01_gaikuang.anchor: the Fuxingshe, which some people also called the Blue Shirts
fm01_gaikuang.note: The tangle of names is real and is not the author's confusion. Chinese Renaissance Society (中华复兴社), Vigorous Practice Society (力行社) and Blue Shirts (蓝衣社) were used for overlapping bodies in a concentric structure built around Chiang Kai-shek by Whampoa graduates from 1932. "Blue Shirts" was largely an outsiders' and journalists' name — it circulated widely in the foreign press of the 1930s, which cast the group as China's fascists — and members themselves rarely used it. Historians have argued since the 1980s about how much of the "Blue Shirt" organization existed as described and how much was inferred from hostile reporting; Shen Zui's casual "some people also called it" is closer to the truth than most contemporary accounts.

fm01_gaikuang.anchor: Inside the Juntong it was known as the Ten-Man Team.
fm01_gaikuang.note: The founding group of Dai Li's service. Rosters differ between accounts, and even the count is not stable — the phrase means "the original ten" rather than a fixed list, and different memoirists name different men among them. Shen Zui joined later and is reporting the service's own founding legend, which by his day was commemorated annually.

fm01_gaikuang.anchor: He Zhonghan, Feng Ti, Teng Jie, Zhou Fu, Kang Ze, Gui Yongqing, Pan Youqiang, Zheng Jiemin and Qiu Kaiji
fm01_gaikuang.note: The Lixingshe's founding council, drawn almost entirely from the Whampoa Military Academy's first class. He Zhonghan and Teng Jie were the principal organizers; Kang Ze ran the propaganda side and the Farmer's Bank militia; Gui Yongqing became a senior field commander. Feng Ti was executed in 1938 for the burning of Changsha, the scorched-earth fire set on a false alarm that destroyed the city and killed thousands — one of the war's worst self-inflicted disasters, for which three officials were shot. That Dai Li appears here only as an alternate member is the point of the paragraph: at the founding he was junior to all of these men, and outlasted nearly all of them.

fm01_gaikuang.anchor: The department was established on 1 April 1932.
fm01_gaikuang.note: The date is well attested and the service kept it as its birthday for the rest of its existence — see the "April the First Assembly" below. The Juntong dated itself from the founding of this secret-service department of a semi-secret society, not from the bureau whose name it later carried.

fm01_gaikuang.anchor: the boss of the CC clique, Chen Lifu
fm01_gaikuang.note: Chen Lifu (1900–2001) and his brother Chen Guofu ran the Kuomintang's party organization and its party-based intelligence service; "CC" is usually explained as the brothers' initials or as "Central Club." The rivalry sketched in this paragraph — party intelligence under the Chens against military intelligence under Dai Li — structures the whole of Nationalist secret-service history, and the 1938 split into Zhongtong and Juntong described further down is its formal settlement.

fm01_gaikuang.anchor: his Whampoa class was a late one — the sixth
fm01_gaikuang.note: The Whampoa Military Academy's intake number functioned as a rank of seniority in its own right throughout the Nationalist officer corps, independent of actual position. Dai Li entered with the sixth class in 1926, years behind the first-class men who founded the Lixingshe, and never lost the handicap; the workaround Shen Zui describes — real power as deputy director, the directorship left to a succession of senior figures who did not exercise it — is the standard account of how it was managed.

fm01_gaikuang.anchor: the Special Political Problems Research Office, run by Zhang Guotao
fm01_gaikuang.note: Zhang Guotao (1897–1979) was a founder of the Chinese Communist Party, present at its first congress in 1921, and commander of the Fourth Front Army; he lost his power struggle with Mao Zedong on the Long March and defected to the Nationalists in April 1938. The Juntong then put him to work against his former party. Nothing else in this chapter's list of offices carries the weight this half-sentence does, and Shen Zui passes over it without comment — a founder of the Communist Party is a line item between a research office and a recreation room. Zhang Guotao later left for Hong Kong and died in Canada. The scan is unambiguous here; the OCR read the name as a nonentity, and it was crop-verified against the page.

fm01_gaikuang.anchor: a Zhongshan Room in charge of recreation
fm01_gaikuang.note: Named for Sun Yat-sen (Sun Zhongshan). Nationalist units maintained a "Zhongshan Room" as a combined reading room, recreation room and political-instruction space — the Nationalist counterpart to the club rooms of other twentieth-century party-armies.

fm01_gaikuang.anchor: the aircraft Dai Li was travelling in flew into Dai Hill
fm01_gaikuang.note: Dai Li died on 17 March 1946 when his aircraft, flying from Qingdao to Nanking in bad weather, struck high ground near Banqiao, south-east of the city. The hill is usually given in Chinese sources as 岱山 Dai Hill or the site as Kunyugou; this book prints 戴山, which is the author's own surname-character for Dai Li himself. The homophone has fed a long afterlife of stories about the coincidence of the name. His death is the hinge of the second half of this book: everything about the Bureau of Secrets Preservation, Zheng Jiemin and Mao Renfeng follows from it.

臭招牌, literally "stinking shop-sign." The idiom is ordinary Chinese for a discredited brand, but the register here is not neutral, and it recurs throughout the book: Shen Zui is writing in the early 1960s, as a pardoned war criminal, for a state publication, about an organization he served in for eighteen years. Where the English keeps expressions like this one, or "criminal activities" and "the reactionaries" below, it is preserving evidence of the conditions the book was written under rather than importing a judgement of its own.

fm02_qianyan.anchor: the first thing I did was to confess my guilt to him
fm02_qianyan.note: 请罪, literally "to beg punishment." Shen Zui had been captured in Yunnan in 1949 and held for eleven years; he was released in the first special amnesty of December 1959, which freed thirty-three war criminals judged to have reformed. The reception described here comes fourteen months later. The confession-first reflex is not a literary flourish: it is the trained posture of a man whose release was conditional on having demonstrated exactly that reflex, and it shapes the whole book.

fm02_qianyan.anchor: Vice-Premiers Chen Yi and Luo Ruiqing
fm02_qianyan.note: Chen Yi (1901–1972), marshal, foreign minister and one of the Communist commanders in the very campaigns that ended Shen Zui's career. Luo Ruiqing (1906–1978) was Minister of Public Security from 1949 to 1959 and by 1961 chief of the general staff: that is, the man who had run the apparatus that held Shen Zui was now in the room receiving him. Neither point is made in the text, and both would be obvious to the book's Chinese readers.

fm02_qianyan.anchor: we had merely served as his unpaid escort
fm02_qianyan.note: 义务随从. The joke lands harder in Chinese, where 义务 means "voluntary, unpaid" in the specific sense used of public-spirited service — Zhou is saying the Juntong's surveillance amounted to a free bodyguard detail. This is the anecdote's governing tone: the Premier is not accusing the man in front of him, he is telling him he was never any good at his job.

The Sun Ya on Nanking Road, opened in 1927, one of the best-known Cantonese establishments in the city and a normal place for a well-dressed man to be seen. Zhou Enlai ran the Communist Party's underground apparatus in Shanghai in the late 1920s and early 1930s, when discovery meant death; the point of the story is that concealment worked best in the most public place available.

fm02_qianyan.anchor: you will have served those who come after as a teacher by negative example
fm02_qianyan.note: 反面教员, "negative-example teacher," a term of art in Chinese political language of the period: a person or thing whose bad example instructs. It was applied to former enemies, to purged officials, and eventually to almost anyone. Here it is the precise job description Zhou Enlai is offering, and it is the commission under which this entire book was written. Every page that follows is shaped by it.

fm02_qianyan.anchor: counts as a further confession, and the government will certainly not call you to account for it
fm02_qianyan.note: The assurance is the hinge of the book's reliability, and it cuts both ways. It removes the strongest reason to conceal — but it also creates an incentive to over-confess, since the value of the testimony to those commissioning it rises with how damning it is. Both pressures should be kept in mind at every point where Shen Zui reports his own crimes.

fm02_qianyan.anchor: what is asked of you is truth, not completeness
fm02_qianyan.note: 要求真实，不求全面. Chen Yi's formula is the editorial charter of the whole Selected Historical Materials project, and it is a genuinely good one for memoir evidence: it asks the witness for what he actually knows rather than for a coherent account, and it explicitly forbids filling gaps. What follows immediately — Chen Yi striking out material that magnified his own part — shows the other edge of the same policy.

fm02_qianyan.anchor: so he had struck all of it out
fm02_qianyan.note: Worth pausing on. In the same breath in which he demands truth and forbids invention, Chen Yi describes deleting accounts of his own guerrilla campaigns because they credited him too much and the Party too little. The standard being set is not simply accuracy; it is accuracy within a frame that requires collective rather than individual agency. That frame operates throughout this book too.

fm02_qianyan.anchor: the seventh day of the lunar year
fm02_qianyan.note: 21 February 1961 was indeed the seventh day of the first lunar month, which is a small but real check on the date: the two calendars agree. The seventh day, 人日 or "Humans' Day," is traditionally the birthday of humankind. Nothing in the text makes anything of that, but it is why the countryside was still keeping the festival.

奉谕速办. This is the sharpest documentary observation in the book, and it is the observation of a man who had the files in his hands. 谕 is the word for a superior's directive and, historically, for an imperial edict; 奉谕 says an order has been received without saying from whom. Shen Zui's point is that the Juntong's killing orders were papered in a formula that recorded authority while naming nobody, so that the archive proves an instruction existed and can never show whose it was. It is a claim about deniability by design, made from the inside, and it is checkable in principle against surviving Nationalist files.

fm02_qianyan.anchor: more than a hundred martyrs were cruelly put to death
fm02_qianyan.note: The Chungking massacre of 27 November 1949, at the Zhazidong and Baigongguan prisons on the eve of the city's fall, in which political prisoners were machine-gunned and the buildings burned. The dead are usually numbered in the low hundreds; the prisons were part of the compound the Sino-American Cooperative Organization had used, which is why the massacre and SACO are permanently linked in Chinese memory. Shen Zui devotes a later chapter to that organization.

fm02_qianyan.anchor: "Child, you may go without office, but you must be a decent human being."
fm02_qianyan.note: 你可以不做官，但要做人. The force of the line is in 做人 — literally "to be/act as a person," meaning to conduct oneself as a human being ought — set against 做官, "to be an official." The pairing makes office and decency alternatives rather than companions. The same phrase supplies the title of the 1980 People's Daily interview reprinted at the end of this book, where Shen Zui says he only learned what 做人 meant after 1949; the preface and the closing piece are bound together by it.

fm02_qianyan.anchor: I have left out the names of some of them, clearly as I remember those names
fm02_qianyan.note: An editorial decision worth noticing, because it is the one place in the preface where Shen Zui says outright that he is withholding something he knows. His stated reason is to protect the relatives; the effect is that the book's account of defectors from the Communist Party is deliberately incomplete in exactly the respect readers would most want to check.

fm02_qianyan.anchor: In 1975, when Zheng Xilin came to Peking on a study visit
fm02_qianyan.note: 1975 is when the last group of imprisoned Nationalist personnel was pardoned, and the "study visits" to Peking were part of that programme. So the verification Shen Zui describes — checking the founding roster with two surviving members of the original group — was possible only because both men had outlived the service, the civil war and twenty-five years of captivity or obscurity. It is also the best evidence in the book of his working method: he checked what he could, with the few people alive who could check it.
